paper_title: LogT: Logically Think with Images for Visual Search

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Thinking with images empowers vision-language models (VLMs) to use an external Zoom-in tool for fine-grained visual search. Recent works employ supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) with tool-specific designs to enable such capabilities. However, achieving logical reasoning alongside accurate and efficient tool use remains a significant challenge. To address this, we shift the focus away from increasing RL complexity and instead identify SFT data quality as a key bottleneck. We then propose LogT (short for Logically Think with Images), a fully automated SFT data engine that explicitly enforces logic-chain-guided reasoning. LogT generates an SFT dataset featuring challenging, visually grounded questions and structured tool-use traces with human-like logic. We validate our approach by fine-tuning two base models, Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL3.5-8B, on the dataset and evaluating them across seven benchmark test sets. We show that LogT-SFT based on Qwen2.5-VL-7B outperforms the state-of-the-art trained with both SFT and RL, despite using 3.1$\times$ less data and $>120\times$ fewer GPU hours. Furthermore, applying a simple RL recipe without tool-specific design on LogT-SFT yields a model that surpasses prior methods with complex RL setups by a substantial 9.59-point margin. In addition to strong performance gains, our model exhibits higher tool-use accuracy and efficiency, as well as more structured and logically consistent reasoning traces, directly validating the effectiveness of our approach.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) (Alayrac et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023) integrate visual and textual information by aligning high-level visual cues with text embeddings via visual encoders and projection layers. However, this alignment process introduces irreversible information loss, causing VLMs to struggle with visually intensive tasks that require fine-grained visual search (Wu and Xie, 2024). Even when augmented with text-based chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning (Wei et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2025a), such limitations persist, as textual reasoning cannot recover missing visual details. Therefore, recent works (Hu et al., 2024; OpenAI, 2025c) introduce thinking with images, enabling VLMs to invoke external tools to extract additional visual information and interleave it with textual reasoning. In this context, we investigate how VLMs can more effectively leverage the widely studied Zoom-in tool (OpenAI, 2025c; Su et al., 2025a; Zhang et al., 2025b; Zheng et al., 2025; Lai et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025c) for visual search. Existing efforts approach this problem through post-training, typically combining supervised fine-tuning (SFT) for cold start with reinforcement learning (RL) driven by outcome-based and tool-related rewards. While these methods have shown promising results, we find that the improvement largely stems from increased familiarity with the tool format gained during post-training. In contrast, enabling VLMs to logically reason about when and how to invoke the tool for accurate region-of-interest identification and efficient inference remains fundamental challenge (OpenAI, 2025b) (see analysis in Section 4.5). While RL with finer-grained step-by-step process supervision using process reward models (PRMs) (Li et al., 2026) has shown early promise in improving reasoning aided by non-visual tools, PRMs for training VLMs to think with images and use Zoom-in effectively and efficiently remain underexplored, largely due to the limited scalability and high compute cost of training dedicated PRMs. Therefore, we shift the focus from designing more complex RL to improving SFT data quality, which we 1 Figure 1 Main idea. We generate reasoning traces based on human-like strategies including (i) direct answering for simple questions, (ii) multi-hop reasoning by focusing on different regions, and (iii) exhaustive search for more difficult cases. For easy questions where the base models average@8 is 1, we synthesize direct answering traces without Zoom-in. Otherwise, we first generate logic chains that specify key tool-use steps and then use them to guide the VLM in synthesizing tool-use reasoning traces. Figure 2 Result highlights. By applying SFT to Qwen2.5VL-7B model using 5.4k to 7.1k of our synthesized data, LogT-SFT surpasses the best-performing Mini-o3-RL on average across seven test sets, while using up to 3.1 less data and >120 fewer GPU hours. With simple RL setup without any tool-specific design, LogT-RL further outperforms baselines by 9.59. identify as key bottleneck. We propose LogT, novel data engine that generates SFT data to teach VLMs to Logically Think with Images for visual search. Importantly, LogT is fully automated and relies solely on open-source models to enhance the quality of SFT data. Each synthesized SFT sample includes visual search question-answer (QA) pair, and the corresponding tool-use reasoning traces. Accordingly, we design LogT to improve the quality of both QAs and reasoning traces. For QA quality, we enrich the VLMs input with detailed visual contexts in addition to the full image, enabling the synthesis of more challenging questions that target fine-grained visual details. We then apply rigorous filtering to retain only high-quality QA pairs. For reasoning trace quality, we first construct logic chains that mimic human problem-solving strategies (e.g., multi-hop reasoning in Figure 1). These logic chains serve as skeletons and outline the key steps needed to solve each visual search task. We then use them to guide the VLM in generating structured and coherent reasoning traces with appropriate tool calls. To demonstrate the effectiveness of LogT, we train Qwen2.5-VL-7B (Bai et al., 2025b) and InternVL3.58B (Wang et al., 2025a) on our synthesized SFT dataset comprising 7.1k high-quality entries. As shown in Figure 2, using 3.1 less data and >120 fewer GPU hours, our SFT-only model (LogT-SFT based on Qwen2.5-VL-7B) outperforms the state-of-the-art (SOTA) open-source model trained by both SFT and RL across seven test sets. We further apply off-the-shelf RL with straightforward outcome-based rewards, and the resulting model outperforms prior methods by at least 9.59 points, despite their reliance on more complex, tool-specific RL strategies. In addition, both our SFT and RL checkpoints achieve better tool-call accuracy and efficiency. human evaluation further shows that our method produces more coherent and higher-quality reasoning traces. In summary, our contributions are threefold: We identify SFT data quality as key bottleneck and introduce LogT, novel data synthesis strategy that generates high-quality SFT data with challenging QA pairs and coherent, human-like reasoning traces. This strategy produces dataset with 7.1k entries. We show that training Qwen2.5-VL-7B solely on our SFT data outperforms prior SOTA models that use both SFT and RL, while also achieving significantly higher data and training efficiency, highlighting the benefit of investing more compute and effort in SFT data quality. We further improve LogT-SFT with simple RL setup without any tool-specific design, underscoring the importance of SFT quality. The resulting model also achieves higher tool-call accuracy, greater tool-call efficiency, and more logically coherent reasoning traces.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Think with images. Thinking with images extends text-only CoT reasoning by allowing VLMs to interleave textual reasoning with visual information extracted via external tools from either the input image or intermediate tool outputs. Some methods (Hu et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025) adopt training-free, modular agent-based design, allowing VLMs (e.g., GPT-4o (Hurst et al., 2024)) to invoke visual tools during inference. In contrast, other approaches, including OpenAIs o3 (OpenAI, 2025c; Huang et al., 2025b,a; Wu et al., 2025), rely on post-training to incentivize VLMs with tool-use capabilities. Among prior work, Zoom-in is one of the most widely used visual tools (OpenAI, 2025c; Su et al., 2025a; Zhang et al., 2025b; Zheng et al., 2025; Lai et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025c; Su et al., 2025b; Zhang et al., 2025c; Liu et al., 2025), showing consistent improvements in visual search (Wu and Xie, 2024). Most methods employ two-stage post-training pipeline of SFT followed by RL. SFT primarily teaches models to invoke Zoom-in and conform to its calling format, which is useful because current VLMs exhibit limited zero-shot tool-use ability. RL then uses outcome-based rewards to further encourage tool usage and format compliance. However, these approaches still face fundamental challenges to train VLMs to reason logically with images and to call Zoom-in both accurately (Liu et al., 2025) and efficiently (OpenAI, 2025b). Li et al . (Li et al., 2025c) improve tool-call efficiency through designing complex RL rewards and rollout strategies, but at the tradeoff of substantial RL compute overhead. RL with process supervision could potentially mitigate these limitations. However, this often requires PRMs (Li et al., 2026). To the best of our knowledge, PRMs tailored for thinking with images remain underexplored, and training such specialized PRMs that meet our requirements is both challenging and very intensive. SFT data for visual reasoning. Building SFT datasets for thinking with images requires reasoning traces that interleave text with images returned by tool calls. This is challenging because most existing SFT datasets for visual reasoning (Lu et al., 2022; Mu et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2025) contain only textual reasoning, without intermediate visual evidence. few datasets (Shao et al., 2024a; Li et al., 2025a) do provide reasoning traces that interleave texts and images using referenced bounding boxes. However, they typically use low-resolution images and include only single bounding box per trace, making them inadequate for high-resolution and fine-grained visual search tasks requiring multi-step tool use. Recent works on thinking with images (Su et al., 2025a; Zhang et al., 2025b; Lai et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025c) release their own SFT datasets. These studies typically generate visual search questions by directly prompting VLMs with full input images. Consequently, the synthesized questions often center on easy-to-search objects. Furthermore, the reasoning traces are usually generated by directly prompting VLMs or agents without careful quality control, and they often lack the human-like logical structure for solving complex problems, as presented in our approach. We also note that, despite the release of datasets and checkpoints in prior work, the data generation engines themselves receive less attention. In contrast, we focus on the data generation strategy itself.

sections.title: 3 Our Data Engine: LogT
sections.content: We propose novel data synthesis framework, LogT, for generating an SFT dataset with high-quality visual search QA pairs and reasoning traces. This dataset is used to enhance VLMs ability to use Zoom-in for fine-grained visual search. Our goal is to train VLMs not only to invoke Zoom-in in the correct format over one or multiple turns, but also to logically think with images and to use Zoom-in accurately and efficiently to identify regions of interest. Figure 3 illustrates the process for generating single-object QA and its corresponding tool-use reasoning trace. Given an image I0 and two object-centric crops that provide contextual (IC) and focused (IF ) views of the target object, the QA generator produces candidate QA pairs, which are then filtered using automatic quality checks. We then pass the generated QAs along with synthesized caption of I0 to logic chain generator, which produces multi-hop chain LM and an exhaustive search chain (LE). One of these chains is selected and used to guide the reasoning trace generator to construct full trace that interleaves textual reasoning with Zoom-in actions. Each Zoom-in call extracts region from I0 or previous crop, resulting in crops denoted as I1 through I3. 3 Figure 3 detailed overview of LogT SFT data synthesis engine. Part 1 (top; Section 3.1) synthesizes visual search QA pairs using the full image (I0) along with rich visual contexts (IC and IF , top left) related to randomly selected target objects. After generating candidate QAs, we apply simple heuristic filter and use VLM-as-a-Judge to ensure quality. Part 2 (bottom; Section 3.2) generates reasoning traces for the selected QA. For easy questions, we directly generate traces without tool calls (omitted here). For other questions, we first create logic chains (LM and LE) based on two human-like strategies. logic chain selector then chooses the more appropriate one, which is subsequently used to guide the synthesis of multi-turn reasoning traces with tool use. While ensuring high data quality, LogT is fully automated and accessible, relying solely on open-source models without needing complex visual agents. In the following sections, we detail the key components of (i) QA pair generation (Section 3.1) and (ii) reasoning trace synthesis (Section 3.2).

sections.title: 3.1 Object-oriented QA Pair Synthesis.
sections.content: Our QA pair synthesis strategy consists of two steps: (i) generating challenging QA pairs using QA generator, and (ii) performing quality control through filter and QA quality judge. Specifically, we use Qwen2.5-VL-72B (Bai et al., 2025b) as the generator and different open-source VLM with 106B parameters as the judge. As preparation, we source high-resolution images from the SA1B dataset (Kirillov et al., 2023), similar to Pixel Reasoner (Su et al., 2025a) and Chain-of-Focus (Zhang et al., 2025b). For each image, SA1B provides bounding boxes representing unnamed objects. Enhance QA generation with object-oriented visual contexts. We generate visual search QA pairs in an objectoriented manner, with each focusing on one or two specific objects within the input image I0. To avoid bias toward easily identifiable objects and increase question difficulty, we first filter out bounding boxes that cover more than 1% of the image area. From the remaining boxes, we randomly select one box for single-object questions, or pair of boxes for relation-based questions. In addition to the full image, we prepare two more crops related to each bounding box: (i) contextual crop IC that is several times larger than the bounding box to capture surrounding visual context, and (ii) focused crop IF that exactly matches the bounding box to capture fine-grained object details. This results in 3 images for single-object and 5 for relation-based questions. We provide the QA generator with these images, detailed generation rules, taxonomy of permissible question types, and in-context examples to produce two candidate QA pairs. The QA generation prompt is shown in Figure 7. QA filtering and selection. We first apply simple rule-based filter to eliminate QAs that violate output format requirements. Then we evaluate the remaining pairs using the QA quality judge to determine whether one or both conform to our quality criteria, including answer correctness, question unambiguity, etc. If neither QA candidate passes, we discard both; if both are valid, the judge selects the better one. To mitigate positional bias of the judge (Shi et al., 2024), we run the evaluation twice with the QA order reversed. We err on the 4 side of caution by accepting QA pair only if it is consistently validated across both evaluations. Compared to prior work, our method produces more challenging and higher-quality questions. We define average@8 as the accuracy obtained by randomly sampling responses eight times at temperature of 0.8. As shown in Figure 11, only 24% of our synthesized questions are perfectly answered by Qwen2.5-VL-7B without tool use, i.e., average@8 = 1, substantially fewer than in existing datasets.

sections.title: 3.2 Logic Chain-driven Reasoning Trace Synthesis.
sections.content: In visual QA tasks, humans typically adopt one of the following reasoning strategies. We leverage these strategies to ensure the logical coherence of generated reasoning traces and to minimize unnecessary tool usage: (i) Direct answering: When the target object is prominent and the question is straightforward, humans can answer directly without intermediate reasoning. (ii) Multi-hop reasoning: For questions requiring indirect visual cues, like What color is the backpack worn by the person?, humans identify intermediate visual anchors (e.g., the person), then refine their focus (e.g., the backpack), reasoning through multiple hops. (iii) Exhaustive search: When the target is difficult to locate and the question lacks clear visual references, such as asking to find person in crowd, humans may divide the scene into several parts and search systematically. For easy questions where Qwen2.5-VL-7B achieves an average@8 of 100% even without requiring tools, we adopt the direct answering strategy to generate more tool-efficient reasoning trace, consisting of single turn without invoking the Zoom-in tool. Otherwise, we simulate the remaining two strategies and synthesize reasoning traces that involve one or more tool calls. This process includes: (i) abstracting these strategies into logic chains using logic chain generator, where each chain consists of sequence of key steps that specify where to focus and which image to zoom into, (ii) selecting the most appropriate logic chain via logic chain selector, and (iii) leveraging the selected logic chain as structured guidance for the reasoning trace generator to produce coherent tool-use reasoning traces. While an ideal system would rely on single VLM to perform all three parts, current open-sourced VLMs often lack the instruction-following reliability and fine-grained reasoning precision required for high-quality logic chain generation. To address this, we use GPT-OSS-120B (OpenAI, 2025a) as the logic chain generator, and the VLM serves as the QA quality judge for both logic chain selection and reasoning trace generation. Logic chain generation and selection. Given an image I0 and QA, we first supply the logic chain generator with the question and VLM-generated image caption as necessary visual context. It then outputs two types of logic chains: one for multi-hop reasoning (LM ) and one for exhaustive search (LE). Each chain comprises sequential steps that identify target object or region (e.g., person or left crowd) and determine which image to zoom into (e.g., the full image I0 or crop returned from previous Zoom-in call, such as I1 or I2 in Figure 3). The logic chain generator must reason over spatial and contextual dependencies. For example, in Figure 3, it needs to decide whether to zoom in gradually, such as identifying the backpack from crop of the person, or to access multiple objects in parallel, such as finding the security gate and the person. Once both logic chains are generated, we pass them along with the full image and question to the logic chain selector. We use it to choose more appropriate chain based on task complexity and tool call efficiency. Reasoning trace synthesis. Next, we prompt the reasoning trace generator to follow the selected logic chain step-by-step, producing reasoning thought and corresponding Zoom-in action at each turn until reaching the final answer. The prompt used for reasoning trace synthesis is shown in Figure 8. Finally, we build an SFT dataset with 7.1k high-quality QAs and reasoning traces. We present example multi-hop reasoning traces in Figure 12 and an example exhaustive search reasoning trace in Figure 9. Tool-use statistics of our synthesized SFT dataset are provided in Section A.3 and visualized in Figure 10. To qualitatively demonstrate that LogT produces higher-quality reasoning traces, we present case study comparing our traces with those from prior work in Section A.4. Finally, we analyze the computational cost of our data engine in Section A.5.

Additional baselines are evaluated in Table 2 and discussed in Section B.3.
sections.content: Benchmarks. We evaluate our method and baselines on the following benchmarks: (i) Fine-grained visual search on high-resolution images: This includes V* (Wu and Xie, 2024), VisualProbe (Lai et al., 2025), and HR-Bench (Wang et al., 2025b). VisualProbe is officially divided into three difficulty levels: easy, medium, and hard. HR-Bench consists of two resolution-based subsets: 4K and 8K. (ii) Out-of-domain visual perception and reasoning beyond visual search: We use MME-RealWorld-Lite (Zhang et al., 2024), which differs substantially from the LogT SFT dataset in both the visual content and the types of tasks involved. This makes it well-suited for assessing models generalization to out-of-domain visual reasoning tasks beyond visual search. MME-RealWorld-Lite is comprehensive benchmark with 1,919 questions covering 43 task types, evaluating general perception and reasoning capabilities of VLMs across diverse scenarios such as OCR, remote sensing, diagram understanding, etc. In total, our evaluation covers seven test sets, accounting for multiple official splits in VisualProbe and HR-Bench. Evaluation details. We use greedy decoding for all evaluated models1 and report pass@1 accuracy to ensure reproducibility. For all open-sourced models without built-in tool usage, we apply CoT prompting using the instruction Please reason step by step. For o3, we report the V* result from its model card and evaluate VisualProbe using medium reasoning effort with the code interpreter tool. Additional evaluation details are provided in Section B.1.

sections.title:
4.2 Implementation Details
SFT implementation. Following prior works, we use Qwen2.5-VL-7B as the base model. We train it on the
SFT dataset synthesized by LogT for 3 epochs using a learning rate of 1e-5 and an effective batch size of 128.
The resulting model is LogT-SFT.
sections.content: RL implementation. We apply off-the-shelf RL to LogT-SFT fine-tuned on 7.1k samples, to investigate how improved cold-start affects post-RL performance. The resulting model is LogT-RL. Our reward function consists of only two terms: correctness reward (rcorrect) and formatting reward (rformat). The correctness reward assigns rcorrect = 1 if the models predicted answer matches the ground-truth, and 0 otherwise. The formatting reward assigns rformat = 0.5 if the model follows the correct format, and 0 otherwise. The total reward is = rcorrect + rformat. For the RL algorithm, we slightly modify standard Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024b) to encourage exploration. Specifically, we remove KL regularization and adopt the clipping-higher strategy recommended by Yu et al . (Yu et al., 2025) for agentic RL to set the upper clipping ratio to 0.315. We sample 8 rollouts per input, and adopt constant learning rate of 1e-6. We use veRL (Sheng et al., 2024) for implementation and run RL for 100 steps. We source RL training data from Mini-o3 (Lai et al., 2025). sections.title: 4.3 Main SFT Results
sections.content: In this section, we report SFT results using Qwen2.5-VL-7B as the base model. We also fine-tune InternVL3.58B (Wang et al., 2025a) on our SFT dataset and present those results in Table 3 of Section B.4. LogT-SFT outperforms all baselines, including those trained with both SFT and RL, while being highly dataand training-efficient. As shown in Table 1, the LogT-SFT model trained on 7.1k synthetic samples generated by our method, surpasses all open-source baselines, including those post-trained with both SFT and RL. Compared to the strongest SFT baseline, Chain-of-Focus-SFT, our model achieves higher performance across 6 out of 7 test sets, with an average gain of 4.59 points. Against the best-performing baseline, Mini-o3-RL, LogT-SFT delivers 1.9-point improvement. Moreover, even when the number of training samples is reduced from 7.1k to 5.4k, LogT-SFT still outperforms all baselines. In comparison, DeepEyes-RL uses 8.7 more data, and Mini-o3-RL uses 3.1 more. Training Qwen2.5-VL-7B on 5.4k SFT samples takes only 3.2 hours on 8A100 GPUs, making it >120 more compute-efficient than the best RL baseline, Mini-o3-RL, in terms of GPU hours. These results underscore the effectiveness of our data engine in producing high-quality SFT training data. LogT-SFT significantly outperforms SFT baselines under equal data budgets. For fair comparison, we evaluate LogT-SFT under matched or lower data budgets. Specifically, we randomly sample 4k and 5.4k subsets from our synthetic dataset, matching the sizes used by Pixel Reasoner and Chain-of-Focus, and then fine-tune Qwen2.5-VL-7B on these subsets. Under equal data constraints, Table 1 shows that LogT-SFT outperforms Pixel Reasoner-SFT by 9.37 points and Chain-of-Focus-SFT by 4.1 points. sections.title: 4.4 Main RL Results
sections.content: Applying off-the-shelf RL on top of LogT-SFT improves performance and generalization, outperforming all baselines by wide margin. In Table 1, we show that applying off-the-shelf RL to the LogT-SFT model further leads to notable improvement of 7.69 points. Remarkably, LogT-RL surpasses all RL baselines by at least 9.59 points, even though those baselines use more sophisticated and tool-specific RL designs. Moreover, it enhances the models generalization ability, achieving performance comparable to the current SOTA on the out-of-domain benchmark MME-RealWorld-Lite. These results highlight that the benefits of high-quality SFT data generated by our method are further amplified when combined with RL. High-quality SFT data from our framework significantly improves the RL performance ceiling. To evaluate the impact of our SFT data engine on the RL performance ceiling, we apply the same RL recipe from Section 4.2 to Qwen2.5-VL-7B and other existing SFT baselines (Su et al., 2025a; Zhang et al., 2025b; Lai et al., 2025). The validation accuracy dynamics in Figure 4 show that initializing RL with LogT-SFT leads to much higher performance than applying RL directly to the base model (zero-RL). In contrast, RL training on prior SFT baselines quickly plateaus after initial gains and often performs no better, or even worse, than zero-RL after 100 steps. These results indicate that SFT data produced by LogT greatly improve the initial policy and substantially raise the RL performance ceiling.

sections.title: 4.5 Analysis on Tool Use and Reasoning Quality
sections.content: Beyond numerical gains, we show that our data engine enables VLMs to think logically with images and use Zoom-in accurately and efficiently. While existing works open-source their training datasets, the SFT data curation pipelines and associated metadata remain unavailable, making apples-to-apples comparisons difficult. Hence, we focus our analysis on the behavior of the post-trained models. We further show that our model can generalize to novel tools in zero-shot manner in Section B.6. Analysis on tool call accuracy. We evaluate the tool accuracy of model response by assessing how well it localizes the intended region(s) of interest via Zoom-in. We first compute the Intersection over Ground-truth (IoG) (Wang et al., 2018) for each Zoom-in call, defined as IoG = G/G, where is the bounding box used in the Zoom-in call and is the corresponding ground-truth box. Next, we consider response as calling the tool accurately if at least one Zoom-in invocation achieves IoG 0.8, as multiple calls may be issued while answering question. Finally, we define models overall tool call accuracy as the percentage of tool-requiring responses that include at least one accurate Zoom-in call. We compute this metric using V*, the only benchmark that provides ground-truth bounding boxes for target regions. Figure 5 shows that LogT-SFT achieves 72.09% tool call accuracy, outperforming both the base model and other SFT baselines. LogT-RL further achieves the highest accuracy of 94.21%. These results show that the 8 Figure 6 Tool call efficiency. We report the average number of tool calls per question across the seven test sets. Despite achieving better performance compared to prior SOTA, LogT-SFT model uses 2.7 fewer tool calls, and LogT-RL uses 2.3 fewer. SFT data synthesized by LogT effectively teaches VLMs to reason and invoke tools accurately. Interestingly, most SFTand RL-trained baselines underperform the base model that invokes Zoom-in in zero-shot manner, except for Mini-o3. Comparing SFT models and their RL-tuned counterparts, we find that while RL improves tool call accuracy, the quality of SFT is critical for achieving strong tool call accuracy after RL. Analysis on tool call efficiency. We evaluate tool call efficiency by measuring the average number of Zoom-in calls used to solve question across all test sets. As shown in Figure 6, the best-performing baseline, Mini-o3-RL, uses an average of 4.3 Zoom-in calls per task. In comparison, while delivering higher performance, LogTSFT and LogT-RL achieve significantly better efficiency, requiring 2.7 and 2.3 fewer calls, respectively. Although other baselines use fewer Zoom-in calls, their performance is considerably lower. These results suggest that the SFT data synthesized by LogT enables VLMs to reason about the necessary steps for solving questions, striking superior balance between tool call efficiency and overall performance. Human evaluation on reasoning quality and logical coherence. To assess whether the SFT data synthesized by LogT enables VLMs to reason logically with images beyond achieving strong benchmark performance, we conduct human evaluation comparing LogT-RL with the prior SOTA (Mini-o3-RL) based on overall benchmark scores and tool-use accuracy. We randomly sample 100 questions from V* and ask three human annotators to compare the responses produced by both models. For each question, annotators select the preferred response based on three criteria: (i) Faithfulness: Does the model answer the question correctly without hallucinating non-existent visual content? (ii) Logical coherence: Does the reasoning follow consistent and logical flow? (iii) Tool efficiency: Does the model arrive at the answer using Zoom-in efficiently? On average, LogT-RL is preferred in 59% of the cases, with tie in 14%, indicating the effectiveness of our data generation approach. Detailed instructions and per-annotator breakdowns are provided in Section B.5. Besides human study, we also present qualitative case study in Section B.7.

sections.title:
4.6 Ablation Study
Ablation on question difficulty. To investigate the impact of question difficulty on SFT training, we split the
7.1k-sample dataset into an easier half and a harder half based on Qwen2.5-VL-7B’s average@8. As shown
in Table 4 (Appendix), the VLM trained on the harder split achieves better performance on V* (+2.09) and
VisualProbe-Hard (+4.72), while showing only a slight drop on the easy and medium subsets of VisualProbe.
These highlight the importance of synthesizing more challenging questions, as described in Section 3.1, to
help the model acquire the ability to tackle more complex tasks.
sections.content: 9 Ablation on logic chain-driven reasoning trace synthesis. To examine the impact of explicitly generating logic chains for each question to guide reasoning trace synthesis, we compare our method to an alternative that uses only fixed in-context examples based on multi-hop and exhaustive search strategies. As shown in Table 5 in the Appendix, incorporating logic chains improves overall performance after SFT and yields substantial gain of 2.87 points after RL. These results suggest that logic chain-driven synthesis is essential for creating higher-quality SFT data that effectively incentivizes logical reasoning and tool-use capabilities in VLMs. Ablation on models used for data synthesis. To verify that our data engines effectiveness stems from the framework design rather than specific large models, we replace the QA generator, the VLM used for QA judging and trace synthesis, and the logic chain generator in Section 3 with much smaller variants: Qwen3-VL-8B (Bai et al., 2025a), Qwen2.5-VL-32B (Bai et al., 2025b), and GPT-OSS-20B (OpenAI, 2025a), respectively. We then re-synthesize 4k SFT samples, train the base model with SFT, and evaluate it on V*, VisualProbe, and HR-Bench. As shown in Table 6 in the Appendix, performance remains nearly unchanged compared with using the original models for synthesizing 4k SFT data. Using these smaller models, generating 7.1k SFT samples requires about 120 GPU hours (30 hours on 4A100), making it over 25 compute cheaper than the RL training of Mini-o3.

sections.title: 5.2 Relationship to Knowledge Distillation
sections.content: The model ablation  (Table 6)  suggests that LogT does not rely on the original large synthesizing models. Moreover, on V*, the 7B model trained on 4k reasoning traces synthesized using Qwen2.5-VL-32B outperforms Qwen2.5-VL-32B itself by 4.18 points. Together, these results suggest that synthesizing-model strength alone does not explain the effectiveness of our data engine, although knowledge distillation (Fu et al., 2025; Hamman et al., 2025) may still contribute to the gains.

sections.title:
5.3 Limitations
The centrality of Zoom-in. In this work, we focus primarily on Zoom-in for two primary reasons. (i) Practical
importance. The zoom-in tool is widely used in visual reasoning tasks. For example, OpenAI’s o3 model
prominently features this tool in its blog (OpenAI, 2025b). Moreover, all thinking-with-image baselines
in Table 1 rely on zoom-in as their sole image interaction mechanism. (ii) Technical challenge. Despite
its prevalence, enabling VLMs to accurately and efficiently decide when and how to invoke the zoom-in
tool remains challenging (see analysis in Section 4.5). OpenAI’s blog (OpenAI, 2025b) similarly identifies
“redundant or unnecessary tool calls and image manipulation steps” as a key limitation of o3.
sections.content: While centered on Zoom-in, our approach demonstrates significant transferability. LogT improves performance on out-of-domain tasks (e.g., MME-RW-Lite in Table 1) and generalizes to unseen tools (Table 8 in Section B.6). 10 More broadly, LogT decouples logic chain synthesis from reasoning trace generation, making it general and extensible framework. This design allows it to be applied to wide range of structured reasoning tasks, and extending LogT to broader domains is promising direction for future work. Reliance on VLM-as-a-Judge. To ensure scalability and avoid costly human annotation, we build fully automated data engine that uses VLM-as-a-Judge. Consequently, the synthesized SFT data may contain small amount of noise, as VLM judges can make mistakes. We view this trade-off as acceptable for two primary reasons. (i) Annotation noise is unavoidable. Errors are not unique to automated judging; they are often inevitable even in expensive human annotations (Vendrow et al., 2025; OpenAI, 2026). (ii) Empirical results and manual verification suggest limited noise. Our method achieves the strongest empirical performance  (Table 1)  and the highest tool-call accuracy (Figure 5), suggesting that any remaining noise is limited and much lower than in prior work. We further randomly sample 100 examples and manually evaluate errors at each stage of the data engine. As shown in Table 7, the error rate at each stage is low despite the fully automated pipeline.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We propose LogT, novel data engine for synthesizing high-quality SFT data that empowers VLMs to logically think with images and use Zoom-in both effectively and efficiently. The core is to generate challenging QAs and high-quality tool-use reasoning traces, guided by logic chains that emulate human-like visual reasoning strategies. VLMs fine-tuned on our synthetic data outperform existing baselines trained with both SFT and RL. Moreover, applying off-the-shelf RL on top of LogT-SFT, without any tool-specific design, further substantially improves performance.

In this example, the target object for the given question, i.e., the pink sign held by the person, is particularly difficult to locate. Therefore, the logic chain selector (see Section 3.2) chooses the exhaustive search logic chain. This logic chain instructs the reasoning trace generator to first zoom in on the crowd and then systematically search the scene from left to right. sections.title: System Prompt for QA Generator
sections.content: You are VisionLanguage assistant tasked with generating one highquality question and corresponding answer for each input image. The purpose is to synthesize QA datasets based on visual content from specific regions in the image. ## Inputs (per task) 1. The input image, with key regions marked by red boxes and larger surrounding areas marked by blue boxes. 2. Annotations, including: Input image size. One or more bounding boxes (indicating key regions). Larger cropped images that include the red bounding boxes. Cropped images that correspond to the red bounding boxes. ## Your task 1. Analyze the full image, the marked regions, and the cropped images. 2. Determine whether the input image and the provided region(s) provide enough information to generate highquality question. 3. If yes, generate one question and its corresponding brief answer. 4. If not, return {valid: false}. ## Rules 1. Location The question must be about the object(s) within the provided red bounding box(es). Be very careful: the target object(s) tied to the answer must lie within the red bounding box, not merely nearby and not just within the larger blue box(es). 2. Type Each question must fit one of the following types: perception_single: attribute of single object (e.g., color, category, material). perception_multi: relationship between multiple objects (e.g., larger/smaller, left/right). counting: count of objects in the entire image, but only if those objects appear in at least one bounding box. ocr: read visible text in the region(s) (e.g., words, numbers, labels). reasoning: interpret visuals that require math or chart understanding. (The remaining 5 longer rules are omitted for brevity.) ## Example questions by type (Example questions are omitted for brevity.) Figure 7 System prompt for the QA generator. The remaining rules and in-context examples are omitted for brevity. A.4 Qualitative Case Study of Synthesized Tool-use Traces We present qualitative comparison of reasoning trace synthesis strategies used by Pixel Reasoner (Su et al., 2025a), Chain-of-Focus (Zhang et al., 2025b), Mini-o3 (Lai et al., 2025), and LogT, as shown in Figure 12. Pixel Reasoner synthesizes multi-turn reasoning traces by deliberately inserting Zoom-in calls that focus on overly broad or incorrect regions. In Figure 12a, the first two Zoom-in calls target completely irrelevant areas. In contrast, LogT generates logic chain that guides the reasoning trace generator to first invoke Zoom-in on the building, then refine the focus onto the target text. In Figure 12b, the Chain-of-Focus SFT trace redundantly zooms in on the shoes for six consecutive steps, despite correctly identifying their location in the first step. In contrast, LogT first generates logic chain that instructs the reasoning trace generator to initially zoom in on the person, then gradually focus on the shoes, and finally answer the question using only two Zoom-in calls. similar issue occurs with the Mini-o3 SFT trace in Figure 12c: although it initially identifies the correct target, it repeatedly invokes Zoom-in and ultimately selects an unrelated region, resulting in total of four Zoom-in calls. By comparison, LogT guides the reasoning trace generator to directly locate the wheels, with the reasoning trace requiring only single Zoom-in call before answering. A.5 Computational Cost Analysis Synthesizing 7.1k samples with LogT requires approximately 960 GPU hours (5 days on 8 A100 GPUs), making it more than 3 compute cheaper than RL training for the Mini-o3 baseline. As shown in Section 4.6, synthesis resource use can be substantially reduced by using smaller model variants without compromising performance. With smaller models, the total resource use drops to approximately 120 GPU hours, making it more than 25 compute cheaper than RL training for Mini-o3.

sections.title: System Prompt for Reasoning Trace Generator
sections.content: You are visual question answering assistant equipped with tool called zoom_in, which crops specified region from an image. ## Input (per task) 1. The input image (image_id: 0). 2. Annotations, including: Groundtruth region(s) shown as red boxes in the input image. Input image size. Cropped image(s) corresponding to the groundtruth region(s). 3. Question. 4. Logic chain describing the sequential regions or relations to inspect. ## Your task 1. Your task is to produce complete, stepbystep reasoning trace that visually derives the answer to question using only what is visible in the provided image. 2. Your reasoning trace must follow the given logic chain, though you must never mention the chain itself in your reasoning text. ## Chain structure 1. Each chain is numbered sequence of steps. 2. Each step follows the format <short noun phrase> (k): The short noun phrase names the region, object, or relation to inspect. The optional (k) is numeric zoom tag indicating which image_id to zoom into. ## Rules You must strictly follow all rules. 1. Simulate visual reasoning from scratch and act as if you only have access to: the original image (without groundtruth region(s)), and the question. Do not mention annotations, groundtruth region(s), or the chain explicitly. Simulate realistic, stepbystep visual discovery process. 2.1. Follow the logic chain exactly (multihop reasoning chain only). Strictly follow every step in the chain in order, no skipping, merging, or reordering. 2.2. Be exhaustive but structured. Search systematically, not randomly (exhaustivesearch chain only). Four broad patches max when scanning large area; examine them in deterministic order. Fully examine each candidate region before moving on. Stop the search only when you confirm the target visually. (The remaining 8 longer rules are omitted for brevity.) ## Examples (Example reasoning traces are omitted for brevity.) Figure 8 System prompt for the reasoning trace generator. Each logic-chain entry of the form short noun phrase(k) specifies target object or region and its source image Ik. Here, I0 is the original image, and Ik for 1 is the crop returned by the k-th Zoom-in call. The reasoning trace generator locates the specified target in Ik, predicts its bounding box, and invokes Zoom-in on that image using the predicted box. For example, Backpack (2) corresponds to Backpack (I2) in Figure 3 and instructs the generator to zoom in on the backpack within the person crop returned by the second tool call. sections.title: B Additional Experiment Setups and Results
sections.content: B.1 Additional Evaluation Details During evaluation, we adopt maximum image resolution budget of 81922828 pixels for models in the Qwen2.5-VL-7B family, where each 2828 patch represents visual token. Images exceeding this budget are downsampled. For comparison, Mini-o3 uses smaller default budget of approximately 25512828 pixels. We observe that Mini-o3 consistently performs better under our higher budget. Therefore, we adopt our budget for all Qwen2.5-VL-7B-based evaluations. B.2 Additional RL Implementation Details We provide additional details on our RL implementation that are not covered in Section 4.2. During RL, to reduce GPU idle time and improve training efficiency, we cap the number of Zoom-in calls at 6. Our RL training data comes from Mini-o3, and we filter out trivial cases by removing any question where Qwen2.5-VL-7B achieves an average@8 of 100%. To monitor training dynamics during RL, we use validation set composed of samples from V*, VisualProbe, and HR-Bench. B.3 Performance Comparison Between LogT and Additional Baselines To further demonstrate the effectiveness of LogT, we evaluate our approach against broader set of baselines. Specifically, we include two more open-source models of comparable scale (7B8B): InternVL3.5-8B (Wang et al., 2025a) and LLaVA-OneVision-7B (Li et al., 2024). We also consider modular-agent frameworks that enable proprietary models to use external tools, such as Visual Sketchpad (Hu et al., 2024) and PyVision (Zhao et al., 2025). In addition, we evaluate two visual-search-based methods that rely on external visual experts: SEAL (Wu and Xie, 2024) and DyFo (Li et al., 2025b). The performance of these baselines, along with LogT-SFT and LogT-RL, is shown in Table 2. Results indicate that both LogT-SFT and LogT-RL significantly outperform the additional baselines, consistent with the findings in Table 1. B.4 SFT Results on an Additional Base Model: InternVL3.5-8B To evaluate whether our data engine generalizes to other base models, we fine-tune InternVL3.5-8B using 7.1k SFT samples generated by LogT. These results suggest that LogT can generalize to novel tasks and previously unseen tools. 22 Figure 15 Qualitative case study comparing model responses to V* question between baseline models and LogT-RL. We show the generated reasoning traces, including Zoom-in calls, for both baseline models and LogT-RL. While Qwen2.5-VL7B-RL, Pixel Reasoner-RL, and Chain-of-Focus-RL produce the correct final answer, their responses contain hallucinations or self-contradictions. The remaining baselines make erroneous Zoom-in calls and ultimately produce incorrect answers. In contrast, LogT-RL follows coherent and consistent reasoning chain: it first identifies the front cabin of the truck, then locates the tissue box, and finally answers the question correctly without hallucinations. B.7 Qualitative Case Study of Model Responses Generated By Baselines and LogT-RL To illustrate how SFT data synthesized by LogT helps VLMs reason logically and use Zoom-in accurately, we present qualitative case study comparing model responses to question from the V* benchmark. These comparisons are shown in Figure 15. We refer to Qwen2.5-VL-7B-RL as the model obtained by directly applying our RL training procedure from Section 4.2 to the base model Qwen2.5-VL-7B. For all other baselines, we use the officially released checkpoints. Qwen2.5-VL-7B-RL answers the question correctly but hallucinates non-existent white text on the tissue box. Pixel Reasoner-RL also produces the correct answer; however, its Zoom-in call targets an irrelevant region, and its final answer contradicts its own statement that There is no tissue box. DeepEyes-RL focuses on white sheets of paper and incorrectly concludes that the tissue box is white. Chain-of-Focus-RL zooms in on an irrelevant region and hallucinates, though it ultimately answers correctly. Mini-o3-RL selects regions that include the tissue box, but still arrives at an incorrect answer. LogT-RL first identifies the likely location of the tissue box (the trucks front cabin), then zooms in on the tissue box itself, ultimately producing the correct answer without any hallucinations. Among all the models, LogT-RL is the only one that reaches the correct answer and shows no hallucinations. This example further demonstrates that our data engine produces high-quality SFT data that effectively trains VLMs to reason about images in logical and faithful manner.
